name: John Ruskin
role: English art critic and social thinker (1819-1900)
summary: Ruskin called himself a violent Tory of the old school and an illiberal, yet also a communist of the old school. He rejected competition and laissez-faire economics, proposing government schools and workshops, fixed wages and state pensions, while opposing equality, universal equal suffrage and liberty as a goal, and favouring kings, hierarchy and obedience to the wise. He held that war and empire can build national virtue, that women and men have complementary roles, and he deplored railways, factories and the division of labour.

sources.usedFor: Summary of his social works, the Guild, his later attack on interest and rent, and his 1884 resignation over vivisection.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: He condemned dividing the worker in manufacture but elsewhere treated division of labour as the basis of exchange and asked for factories supplying pure goods.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: He thought it highly advantageous that persons distinguished by race should set examples of wise expenditure and wanted kings and bishops kept.

alienated-labor.rationale: He described the division of labour as splitting men into fragments so that their intelligence is spent on a pin's point, and called for work that ennobles the workman.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The Creed of his Company vows not to kill or hurt any living creature needlessly, and he left his Oxford chair in 1884 over a vivisection laboratory.

ban-interest.rationale: He thought lending for gain sinful in the abstract and later sided with those condemning interest, but said repression by law would fail and kept taking interest himself.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: He said the state should organise protection in childhood and old age and that a pension from the nation or parish is an honourable reward, not alms.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: He said English rule in India is valuable if it exalts the native race and welcomed colonies guiding distant nations from savageness to manhood.

conscription.rationale: He said that pressing a sailor or seizing a youth by conscription may be right or wrong according to need.

consent-of-governed.rationale: He wanted no liberty but instant obedience to known law and appointed persons, with authority resting on wisdom rather than consent.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: He wanted public provision for the poor and the old to be large and not disgraceful, and thought the state should protect age as a debt owed.

democracy-best.rationale: He called himself a violent illiberal, rejected universal equal suffrage and mocked majority rule as cockchafer democracy.

direct-votes.rationale: He mocked decisions by universal suffrage and wanted government by the wise.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: In Of Queens' Gardens he assigns man the active, defensive public role and woman the ordering, comforting one, in complementary roles.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: He spoke of the true Dei Gratia or divine right of every king as graciousness joined with majesty, and had Companions obey rulers when consistent with God's law.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He declared a sincere love of kings and said Kings should keep their crowns, and he swore his Guild's members to obey the monarch. (Moved from monarchy-legitimate, 2026-11-11, when that statement became about ceremonial heads of state.)

equal-outcomes.rationale: He wrote that if one point is insisted on throughout his works it is the impossibility of equality and the eternal superiority of some men to others.

experts-over-public.rationale: He held that the wiser should lead and wanted votes weighted by age, wisdom, and office.

family-wage.rationale: He asked for a legal wage that buys the food and lodging needed for a labourer's healthy life, with further laws for the maintenance of families.

free-trade.rationale: He called himself an utterly fearless free trader, said every wise nation will open its ports and that opening should be gradual.

gradual-change.rationale: He told workmen to hold their reforms as objects of patient purpose and not to enforce them suddenly, yet he wished to destroy railways and change much.

harm-principle.rationale: He called himself illiberal, detested every approach to liberty and ridiculed Mill's Essay on Liberty.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: He said wealth should be the reward of sagacity and industry rather than of luck, and that great riches come from taxing the labour of others.

job-guarantee.rationale: In his political creed anyone out of work is to be received at the nearest government school or workshop and set to work at a fixed wage.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: He called government and co-operation the laws of life and anarchy and competition the laws of death, and attacked the gospel of supply-and-demand and laissez-faire.

moral-incentives.rationale: He held that the merchant's fee, like a pastor's stipend or physician's honorarium, is not the object of his life, which is to provide for the nation, even at a cost to himself.

municipal-businesses-mixed-economy.rationale: He proposed government manufactories and shops selling honest goods beside private trade, which could 'beat the Government if they could'.

natural-rulers.rationale: He wrote that he aimed to show the eternal superiority of some men to others and the case for appointing them to guide, lead and even compel their inferiors.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: He wrote that inherited wealth involves the most definite responsibilities and that the rich owe care to the poor.

pay-for-effort.rationale: He argued that all labour should be paid at one fixed rate, with the good workman chosen and the bad left unemployed, rather than pay set by each worker's output.

physical-labour-duty.rationale: His Guild's Companions pledge to labour for their daily bread and to do manual cultivation, and he wanted none idle but the dead.

profit-exploitation.rationale: He wrote that no man becomes largely rich by his own toil and that opulence comes from a method of taxing the labour of others and appropriating its profits.

property-franchise.rationale: He would give every adult man without a conviction a vote but weight votes by age, income and office, which is not a property bar.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: He praised manual work on the land and honest country people, wished to destroy the new town of Edinburgh and New York, and founded his Guild on farming.

school-vouchers.rationale: His plan has the nation's children pass through government schools at government cost, not through schools chosen with public money.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: He spoke of a true wifely subjection, the woman's power being guiding rather than determining.

state-harmful.rationale: He wrote that government and co-operation are the laws of life.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He listed protection among mischievous practices and wanted existing protections lifted by degrees.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: He dismissed boasted progress, saying faster travel and increased production are small gains for people not made happier, and wanted to destroy most railways.

territorial-expansion.rationale: He told Oxford that England must found colonies as fast and as far as she is able, seizing every piece of fruitful waste ground.

war-builds-character.rationale: In 'War' he said war is the foundation of all the arts and high virtues and that nations are born in war and expire in peace, though not all war does this.

work-for-welfare.rationale: His scheme sets those who object to work to the hardest forms of necessary toil under strict compulsion; relief goes with labour.

notes: Sources: his own books and letters (Gutenberg texts of Unto This Last, Crown of Wild Olive with Munera Pulveris, Time and Tide, Fors Clavigera vols 1-5, Sesame and Lilies, Lectures on Art, Stones of Venice) plus the 1911 Britannica. Themes searched without finding a stated position: healthcare, taxation, unions as such, immigration, race, abortion, sexuality, drugs, nuclear power, climate. His views shifted little from Unto This Last (1860-62) to Fors Clavigera (1871-84); from 1876 he attacked interest and rent in earnest (s12), but his earlier note on usury already leaned the same way. The Fors Clavigera volumes after vol. 5 were not read in full.
